title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC mandate vs threat; divine will beyond Scripture tip
pass_a_gloss: Add the asymmetry: on that scheme the command would belong to Adam as race-head while the threat belonged to him as a private person—and for us the threat would reach us without the command. Why was the covenant not struck so that as he sinned he was also punished as head of the race? If you fall back on the divine will, every knot gets the same general answer—because God so willed. But take care not to ascribe to Him a will cut to your own ingenuity, least fitting His virtues, and beyond Scripture.
pass_b_english: Add that on that account the command would have belonged to Adam one way, the threat another: the former as to the head of the human race, the latter as to a private person; and conversely the threat would have belonged to us, not likewise the command. Finally, why was that covenant not contracted on this condition, that as he sinned, so also he should be punished as head of the human race? If you fall back on the will of God, what need was there of any other answer to these questions than that general one, because God so willed? But see that you do not ascribe to Him a will suited to your own ingenuity, least fitting to His virtues, and beyond Scripture.
source_text: Adde quod ea ratione aliter ad Adamum pertinuisset mandatum, aliter comminatio: illud ut ad caput generis humani, haec ut ad privatam personam: & vice versa ad nos pertinuisset comminatio, non item mandatum. Denique cur non ea conditione contractum est istud foedus, ut quemadmodum peccaret, sic etiam puniretur ut caput generis humani? Si recurras ad voluntatem Dei, quid opus erat ad has quaestiones alia responsione, quam generali ista, quia Deus ita voluit? Sed vide ne ei voluntatem attribuas pro tuo ingenio eius virtutibus minime convenientem, ac praeter Scripturam.

choices.choice: Command/threat asymmetry; bare 'God willed' risks unscriptural will
